title: Software did not trade as one AI story
summary: Growing AI use did not guarantee faster revenue growth across nine software companies.
watch: Whether Salesforce pilots and ServiceNow AI interest turn into production revenue.

chart.alt: Small-multiple price charts, one per company (CRM, TEAM, NOW, PLTR, CRWD, PANW, ZS, ADBE, INTU), each against QQQ and rebased to 100.

thesis: AI created different opportunities and constraints across software companies. Later customer checks supported workflow demand but exposed barriers between AI interest, production adoption and revenue. Company evidence and matched price windows clarify the split without proving what caused returns.
chartNote: Q3 rebounds did not erase earlier drawdowns: CRM, TEAM, NOW and PLTR all still lagged QQQ year to date.
note: Price moves provide context; they do not establish what caused a return.

items.label: Sep 16–29, 2026 · CRM: core demand improved, AI conversion lagged
items.text: Dreamforce checks supported core demand and headless workflows, but Jefferies and Oppenheimer found pricing, data readiness and pilots constraining monetization. CRM returned +46.8% in Q3 and −10.8% year to date, versus QQQ +22.4% year to date.

items.label: Aug 7–Sep 14, 2026 · TEAM: seats and usage pricing are different tests
items.text: Seat expansion supported August results; Mizuho later expected price increases and usage billing to add growth, with monetization still prospective. TEAM returned +130.5% in Q3 and +15.9% year to date, versus QQQ +22.4% year to date.

items.label: Sep 15–Oct 2, 2026 · NOW and PLTR: demand meets delivery constraints
items.text: UBS found PLTR delivery bottlenecks; JPMorgan found strong NOW renewals but costs and governance delaying AI production. NOW and PLTR returned +35.0% and +60.3% in Q3 and −12.3% and +6.2% year to date, versus QQQ +22.4% year to date.

items.label: Apr 22–Sep 28, 2026 · Cybersecurity: platform demand, separate execution risks
items.text: Wells favored PANW and CRWD platform demand; BTIG forecast PANW growth, while ZS changed sales leadership with competition unresolved. CRWD, PANW and ZS returned +130.4%, +118.9% and −12.6% year to date, versus QQQ +22.4%.

items.label: Sep 11–14, 2026 · ADBE and INTU: adoption versus acquisition
items.text: Adobe needed incremental AI monetization; JPMorgan later highlighted Intuit customer-addition weakness and reliance on revenue per customer. ADBE and INTU returned +17.0% and +6.1% in Q3 and −32.1% and −57.2% year to date, versus QQQ +22.4% year to date.

sections.heading: The strongest case on each side

items.label: Support
items.text: Core workflow demand, seat expansion, renewals and platform consolidation support distinct company cases. Broker checks and forecasts are not independently verified outcomes.

items.label: Challenge
items.text: Pilots, implementation capacity, token costs and weak customer acquisition can prevent interest from becoming durable revenue. A rebound cannot settle those tests.

sections.heading: What to watch and how to update the view

items.label: Enterprise applications
items.text: If CRM pilots, TEAM paid usage, NOW production adoption and PLTR delivery capacity improve, strengthen each company case separately.

items.label: Security
items.text: If PANW forecasts convert to results, CRWD bookings grow and ZS execution improves after its leadership transition, strengthen each case separately.

items.label: Laggards
items.text: Incremental AI monetization would strengthen Adobe; recovering customer additions would support Intuit. Adoption or price gains alone leave these tests open.

notes.text: Dates show when each source was available; publication times may be unknown.

items.label: The starting view
items.text: Goldman rated Salesforce and ServiceNow Buy, but Adobe Sell. It expected AI to benefit software companies differently.

items.label: What was already known
items.text: That split already argued against treating all software companies as the same AI bet.

items.label: What changed
items.text: Dreamforce checks found improving core Salesforce demand but slow AI conversion. JPMorgan later found healthy ServiceNow renewals with costs and governance delaying production adoption.

items.label: The open question
items.text: Can interest and pilots become durable revenue after deployment, cost and customer-acquisition constraints?

title: Meta’s AI products still need to earn their keep
summary: Meta’s AI investment case depends on covering spending commitments beyond its reported capital budget.
watch: Disclosed Muse revenue, which would support payback; Morgan Stanley expects meaningful monetization to take years.

chart.alt: Price chart of META against QQQ, rebased to 100, with numbered turning points: 1. Jul 28, 2025 Superintelligence Labs chief named; 2. Oct 29, 2025 Q3 guide lifts capex; 3. Jan 28, 2026 2026 capex guide; 4. Apr 8, 2026 Muse Spark released; 5. Apr 27, 2026 Manus unwind ordered; 6. Jul 30, 2026 Q2 results; 7. Sep 9, 2026 Muse adoption takes off.

thesis: Meta’s advertising business is benefiting from AI, while its rebuilt models and new products offer another route to growth. The investment question is whether those benefits can cover the cost of its expanding AI commitments.
chartNote: Full history: Jun 26, 2025–Oct 2, 2026: META +0.7%, QQQ +38.0%; 37.3 percentage points behind QQQ.
note: Price moves provide context; they do not establish what caused a return.

notes.text: These themes overlap in time; each date range identifies the sources for that theme.

items.label: Jun 12–Oct 16, 2025 · Meta hired leaders and reorganized research
items.text: Meta named Zhao chief scientist of Superintelligence Labs, planned another reorganization and hired senior researchers after Alexandr Wang joined.

items.label: Jun 27–Oct 29, 2025 · Better ads, bigger spending plans
items.text: Piper reported better ad conversions from recommendations; Meta later raised its capital-spending guidance. On Oct 30, 2025, from the Oct 29 close, META fell 11.3% and QQQ fell 1.5%.

items.label: Jan 26–Apr 29, 2026 · Meta raised spending plans twice
items.text: Meta raised spending plans in January and April; the shares rose after one report and fell after the other. On Jan 29, 2026, META rose 10.4% and QQQ fell 0.6%; on Apr 30, META fell 8.6% and QQQ rose 0.9%.

items.label: Jan 7–May 21, 2026 · China ordered Meta to unwind Manus
items.text: China ordered Meta to unwind its purchase of Manus, an AI-agent developer; its founders reportedly explored financing a buyback, with completion unconfirmed.

items.label: Apr 8–Jun 3, 2026 · Meta released Muse Spark
items.text: Meta launched Muse Spark, its rebuilt AI model; brokers saw progress, but the Financial Times later reported reused Llama code and data and weaknesses in coding.

items.label: Jul 6–30, 2026 · Ad growth faced rising costs
items.text: July results showed advertising growth alongside pressure on margins and cash flow; analysts disagreed over computing costs. On Jul 30, 2026, from the Jul 29 close, META fell 8.0% and QQQ rose 3.3%.

items.label: Sep 9–Oct 2, 2026 · Product adoption raised the revenue question
items.text: Muse usage and commerce features grew, but Morgan Stanley expected monetization to take time; Needham questioned returns after including broader spending commitments.

sections.heading: The strongest case on each side

items.label: Support
items.text: Meta grew advertising revenue, launched Muse Spark and attracted users to Muse.

items.label: Challenge
items.text: Meta faces an ordered Manus unwind, weaknesses in coding and spending commitments that raise the cost of earning a return.

sections.heading: What to watch and how to update the view

items.label: Commercial use
items.text: Watch for Meta to disclose Muse subscription or transaction revenue: growing sales would support payback; usage without sales would leave it unproven.

items.label: Model delivery
items.text: Watch independent tests of Muse Spark’s coding and task performance: sustained gains would support Meta’s rebuild; persistent weaknesses would challenge it.

items.label: Investment economics
items.text: Compare Meta’s reported advertising gains and AI revenue with cash spending and commitments: benefits catching up would support payback; costs pulling ahead would weaken it.

notes.text: Dates show when each source was available; publication times may be unknown.

items.label: The starting view
items.text: Evercore saw Muse, Meta’s consumer AI agent, winning users after its app-store success.

items.label: What was already known
items.text: Wolfe flagged weak trust in sharing payment details. Amazon blocked access, showing that gaining users did not guarantee access to their shopping.

items.label: What changed
items.text: StoneX thought subscriptions would mostly cover computing costs. Morgan Stanley later pushed meaningful revenue further out, separating popularity from profit.

items.label: The open question
items.text: Will users make purchases through Muse, and will the resulting revenue justify its serving costs?

title: Optical demand is strong; future profits face harder tests
summary: Possible restrictions on next-generation optical imports could favor Lumentum and Coherent, but remain a proposal.
watch: Adopted rules and covered products. A proposal alone does not change near-term sales.

chart.alt: Price chart of LITE, COHR against QQQ, rebased to 100, with numbered turning points: 1. Oct 13, 2025 Aletheia initiates on scarcity; 2. Jan 20, 2026 Rebuttal on wafer supply; 3. Apr 9, 2026 JPM raises post-OFC forecasts; 4. Jun 10, 2026 Interim optical designs defended; 5. Aug 11, 2026 LITE reports upside; 6. Sep 24, 2026 PhotonLink value questioned; 7. Oct 1, 2026 Analysts question policy gains.

thesis: Lumentum’s earnings supported the case for tight laser supply and stronger pricing. Investors must now separate delivered profits from forecasts for new optical connections, added factory capacity and possible restrictions on competing imports.
chartNote: Full history: Oct 10, 2025–Oct 2, 2026: LITE +625.5%, COHR +203.4%, QQQ +27.8%; LITE 597.7 percentage points ahead of QQQ, COHR 175.6 ahead.
note: Price moves provide context; they do not establish what caused a return.

items.label: Oct 13–Dec 5, 2025 · Faster connections supported laser pricing
items.text: Aletheia expected faster connections and higher laser prices to lift earnings; December analysts added scarce indium phosphide wafers and optical circuit switching (OCS), which routes light between connections, to the growth case.

items.label: Jan 9–20, 2026 · Analysts disagreed over wafer supply
items.text: Rosenblatt flagged dependence on wafer supplier AXT (AXTI); Aletheia cited alternatives and better economics for faster electro-absorption modulated lasers (EMLs).

items.label: Mar 18–Apr 10, 2026 · Forecasts ran ahead of confirmed orders
items.text: UBS expected connections between racks (scale-out) before connections within computing systems (scale-up); Lumentum’s chief executive projected enough orders to fill 2028 capacity within two quarters, without claiming those orders were secured.

items.label: May 28–Jul 16, 2026 · Analysts debated new connection designs
items.text: Reports questioned co-packaged optics (CPO) timing; others defended near-packaged optics (NPO) and removable modules as interim designs, while the newsletter questioned stagnant earnings estimates and added capacity.

items.label: Aug 4–11, 2026 · Lumentum delivered stronger earnings
items.text: Brokers questioned the scope and feasibility of possible Chinese-product restrictions; Lumentum then beat margin and earnings expectations and raised guidance.

items.label: Sep 22–Oct 1, 2026 · New products and import rules divided analysts
items.text: Stifel favored Coherent’s PhotonLink optical connection technology; other analysts questioned its value, while proposed 3.2T (3.2 terabits per second) import restrictions drew disagreement over near-term benefits.

sections.heading: The strongest case on each side

items.label: Support
items.text: Lumentum beat earnings and margin expectations and raised guidance, supporting the case for tight laser supply.

items.label: Challenge
items.text: Added factory capacity could weaken pricing, while delayed products and Coherent’s sales mix could limit profits.

sources.name: COHR management at a JPM fireside

sections.heading: What to watch and how to update the view

items.label: Delivery and margins
items.text: Check Lumentum’s and Coherent’s reported shipments and margins separately: sustained pricing gains would support tight supply; weaker margins would challenge that benefit.

items.label: Architecture milestones
items.text: Watch announced customer wins and shipments for new optical connections: delivery on schedule would support growth forecasts; delays would weaken them.

items.label: Policy
items.text: Watch for adopted import rules that name products and timing: restrictions covering competing products would support the policy case; narrow or delayed rules would limit it.

sources.name: A chat participant quoted by the newsletter

notes.text: Dates show when each source was available; publication times may be unknown.

items.label: The starting view
items.text: JPM raised Lumentum forecasts for co-packaged optics (CPO), optical circuit switches (OCS) and networking between AI processors.

items.label: What was already known
items.text: UBS expected adoption between processors later than between racks. Optical products had different sales timelines.

items.label: What changed
items.text: June’s dispute questioned CPO’s readiness. August brought stronger margins and earnings: current performance and future technology needed separate checks.

items.label: The open question
items.text: Will laser demand stay strong if customers choose near-packaged rather than co-packaged optics?

title: Reddit’s ads are growing faster than its audience
summary: Reddit’s advertising grew strongly, while third-party tracking pointed to weaker daily user growth.
watch: Reported daily users: stronger growth would challenge the weak tracking; a miss would reinforce the audience concern.

chart.alt: Price chart of RDDT against QQQ, rebased to 100, with numbered turning points: 1. Jul 28, 2025 DAU growth stabilizes; 2. Oct 9, 2025 ChatGPT citation risk; 3. Apr 2, 2026 Licensing pitched as engine; 4. May 1, 2026 Q1: ads strong, users flat; 5. Jul 31, 2026 Ads grow; fewer US users; 6. Sep 16, 2026 App versus search divergence; 7. Oct 2, 2026 Latest traffic and downloads.

thesis: Reddit earns more from advertising while its reliance on Google visitors raises questions about repeat use. Licensing its conversations to AI companies offers another revenue stream, but larger contracts and lasting audience growth still need evidence.
chartNote: Full history: Jul 25, 2025–Oct 2, 2026: RDDT −1.2%, QQQ +33.1%; 34.3 percentage points behind QQQ.
note: Price moves provide context; they do not establish what caused a return.

items.label: Jul 28, 2025 · Ad revenue per user supported recovery
items.text: Jefferies saw daily active user (DAU) growth stabilizing around 13%, with performance advertising and average revenue per user (ARPU) supporting recovery.

items.label: Oct 9–Nov 25, 2025 · ChatGPT visibility fell, then recovered
items.text: Reddit appeared less often in ChatGPT answers, raising concerns about referrals and bargaining power; November tracking showed better visibility and US usage, without measuring licensing revenue.

items.label: Apr 2–May 26, 2026 · Licensing offered growth; search posed a risk
items.text: Analysts expected more licensing revenue while Google’s AI summaries threatened visits; RBC argued prominent links could help referrals, but larger contract renewals remained forecasts.

items.label: May 1, 2026 · Ads grew while logged-in users stalled
items.text: Q1 revenue rose 69% and advertising 74%, but US logged-in daily users rose only 1%, leaving repeat use a concern.

items.label: Jul 31, 2026 · Strong ads accompanied fewer US users
items.text: Q2 ads grew 64%, yet US daily users fell sequentially as Google referrals weakened; management reported better new-app-user retention but stopped separating logged-in and logged-out users.

items.label: Sep 8–16, 2026 · A larger Google deal remained unsigned
items.text: Wells estimated a $250–300 million annual Google deal that remained unsigned; other sources disputed its bargaining-power concerns, while app tracking improved and Google referrals weakened.

sources.name: A chat participant quoted in the wrap

items.label: Oct 1–2, 2026 · Traffic measures gave different signals
items.text: Guggenheim tracked weaker Google traffic and recovering downloads; positive revenue chatter was unverified, and Reddit’s targeting-model change made advertising-reach comparisons unreliable.

sections.heading: The strongest case on each side

items.label: Support
items.text: Reddit’s advertising grew strongly, and licensing its conversations gives it another way to earn revenue.

items.label: Challenge
items.text: Reddit relies on Google referrals, repeat use remains uncertain, and larger licensing renewals remain unsigned.

sections.heading: What to watch and how to update the view

items.label: Repeat engagement
items.text: Watch comparable reports of app use and user retention: more returning users with steady ad returns would support audience growth; falling retention would weaken it.

items.label: Contract economics
items.text: Watch for signed licensing renewals with disclosed payments: larger contracts would support revenue growth; weaker terms would challenge it.

items.label: Traffic conversion
items.text: Compare Google referral tracking with reported daily users and app use: replacing lost visitors with regular users would support lasting growth; continued audience losses would weaken it.

notes.text: Dates show when each source was available; publication times may be unknown.

items.label: The starting view
items.text: Reddit reported strong advertising growth and better results for advertisers.

items.label: What was already known
items.text: The same report showed weak growth in US logged-in users. Better advertising results did not mean Reddit was attracting more regular users.

items.label: What changed
items.text: July brought strong ad growth but falling US users. Reddit reduced user disclosures, making it harder to track the audience behind that revenue.

items.label: The open question
items.text: Will Google renew on better terms, and will consistent user measurements show lasting audience growth?

title: AI spending: four companies, different paths to payback
summary: Analysts see stronger Google products, Microsoft demand and AWS pricing; Meta monetization and investment obligations remain open tests.
watch: Recognized profit and cash after investment and lease commitments across all four companies.

chart.alt: Small-multiple price charts, one per company (GOOGL, MSFT, AMZN, META), each against QQQ and rebased to 100.

thesis: AI demand strengthened, but the path from spending to cash differs across Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta. Later checks add product, pricing and financing evidence without establishing a comparable return on AI investment.
chartNote: All four lagged QQQ over both windows; the returns describe price paths, not AI efficiency or causal effects.
note: Price moves provide context; they do not establish what caused a return.

sections.heading: Four paths from demand to cash

items.label: A common baseline, different accounting.
items.text: Early growth forecasts gave way to component inflation and funding concerns before stronger July results. The tables retain the same June-quarter filings: cloud scopes differ, Azure profit is undisclosed, AWS includes noncash energy gains, and Meta advertising is a separate comparator. September/October checks are not newer reported results.

items.label: Alphabet: product strength versus commercial conversion.
items.text: Google's server-payback claim remains management's assertion. Citi sees Gemini Argon supporting Cloud and product demand, but introductory pricing and benchmark strength do not prove profit. The archive also questions deployment and consumer-agent execution; consolidated cash after investment remains distinct from Cloud or AI returns.

sources.name: Newsletter author with an attributed investor view

items.label: Microsoft: growth checks without a cash upgrade.
items.text: Wells expects stronger Azure growth and improving Copilot adoption, partly supported by seat discounts tied to consumption commitments. Its margin and cash-flow outlook barely changed; separate capacity checks had moderated. Microsoft's earlier apparent spending reduction largely reflected accounting, so adoption and capex headlines alone cannot establish payback.

items.label: Amazon: pricing power and financing costs.
items.text: Wells sees AWS reservation-price increases offsetting inflation, with contracted capacity delaying recognized revenue. The FT reports GPU sale-and-leaseback talks, not a completed transaction. Financing deployed equipment changes funding and future lease obligations; it does not itself improve compute economics or establish incremental AI cash returns.

items.label: Meta: adoption before direct monetization.
items.text: Morgan Stanley expects little direct Muse monetization near term despite usage and enterprise potential. Needham highlights uncommenced leases and other obligations omitted from simple valuation measures. Advertising supports today's business, but serving costs, commercial adoption and commitments determine whether new AI demand earns an adequate return.

items.label: Recognized revenue and profit
items.text: If paid usage converts into incremental profit after serving costs, strengthen payback confidence; separate ads, cloud consumption, subscriptions and hardware.

Until matched investment and cash-flow cohorts are disclosed, there is no defensible single AI-return winner.

items.label: The starting view
items.text: BofA thought Meta could build computing capacity more cheaply.

items.label: What was already known
items.text: Benchmark still saw no path to profit. Component inflation meant higher spending did not necessarily buy more capacity.

items.label: What changed
items.text: Later checks supported Google products, Microsoft demand and AWS pricing, while Meta monetization remained early and financing obligations drew scrutiny.

items.label: The open question
items.text: Will recognized revenue and incremental profit cover investment and lease commitments across all four companies?

title: Memory and storage: shared demand, different supply risks
summary: AI connects DRAM/HBM, NAND and HDD demand; contracts, customer budgets and competing capacity separate supplier outcomes.
watch: Qualified supply, contract margins and customer budgets across the sector. The chart shows SanDisk only.

chart.alt: Price chart of SNDK against QQQ, rebased to 100, with numbered turning points: 1. Jul 13, 2026 Evercore raises target; 2. Jul 28, 2026 Korea memory rout; 3. Jul 30, 2026 Liquidation reported; 4. Aug 14, 2026 13F shows June stake; 5. Sep 22, 2026 Recovery noted (source-reported).

thesis: AI workloads connect memory and storage, but supplier economics diverge. SanDisk belongs within a cycle spanning DRAM/HBM, NAND and HDD; contracts, competing capacity and customer budgets matter more than a shared stock rebound.
chartNote: Jul 29–Oct 2: SNDK +69.3%, QQQ +13.4%; 55.9 percentage points ahead of QQQ. SanDisk comparison only, not a sector return. Endpoints are chosen in hindsight from the July trough.
note: Price moves provide context; they do not establish what caused a return.

items.label: One workload, several storage tiers.
items.text: Evercore expects persistent agents to need fast HBM/DRAM, NAND for cached state, and HDDs for logs. This links suppliers without making them interchangeable; Bernstein expects capacity growth and constrained AI budgets eventually to weaken scarcity pricing.

items.label: DRAM/HBM: unequal supplier execution.
items.text: Bernstein saw Samsung gaining HBM momentum while SK Hynix faced shipment timing delays. Micron reported NAND-led upside but a weaker margin guide; HBM mix, costs and contract terms complicate the growth story. Cleanroom plans are not immediate wafer output.

items.label: NAND: visibility meets customer budgets.
items.text: SanDisk's CFO described broader contracts and node-driven supply growth. Kioxia's CEO warned that steep NAND increases could damage customers' finite AI budgets. Contracts may cushion the cycle, but neither supplier can assume unlimited pricing power.

items.label: China: capital is not qualified capacity.
items.text: CXMT's Shanghai listing preceded reported DRAM fab plans and board-approved R&D/testing investment requiring shareholder approval. Limited PC adoption is not HBM qualification. Separately, YMTC's reported NAND IPO ambitions threaten future NAND supply; neither firm's announced spending proves realized output.

items.label: HDD: shared demand, different competitive risks.
items.text: Bernstein favored Seagate's HAMR transition over WDC's slower path. Both face Toshiba's reported expansion plan, which challenges durable scarcity but takes time to deliver. HDD capacity and NAND substitution can change the benefits of shared AI demand.

sections.heading: What to watch and how to update the view

items.label: Contracts and costs
items.text: If realized pricing and margins hold as spot prices slow, contract durability strengthens.

items.label: Supply and qualification
items.text: If new qualified bits or HDD capacity outpace demand, reduce scarcity assumptions; watch HBM qualification and customer approvals.
July's Korean-memory weakness and reported liquidation matter to SanDisk, but the June-end holding disclosure cannot prove a later sale. Shared demand does not imply equal returns.

notes.text: Dates show when each source was available; publication times may be unknown.

items.label: The starting view
items.text: Evercore expected SanDisk’s contracts to make earnings less dependent on commodity prices.

items.label: What was already known
items.text: Samsung had already disappointed investor expectations despite tight memory supply. Strong industry demand did not guarantee results would clear a high bar.

items.label: What changed
items.text: Later evidence added SanDisk contract claims, Kioxia's pricing restraint, Micron's mixed margin outlook and Toshiba's planned HDD expansion.

items.label: The open question
items.text: Can contract pricing withstand added qualified supply and customer budget limits across distinct DRAM, NAND and HDD markets?

title: One session, two ad-tech results, two separate questions
summary: One session, two ad-tech results: AppLovin faced execution questions while Unity’s Grow and Vector progress drew attention.
watch: Advertiser sign-ups: more would have supported AppLovin’s expansion; stalled sign-ups would have weakened it.

chart.alt: Bar chart of one-session returns for APP, U and QQQ.

thesis: AppLovin and Unity reported into different expectations. APP’s results raised questions about scaling its e-commerce advertiser push, while Unity’s Grow and Vector growth met earlier checks; the session did not isolate how much advertising drove either move.
chartNote: Aug 5–6: APP −19.7%, U +15.1%, QQQ −0.4%; APP 19.3 percentage points behind QQQ, U 15.5 ahead.
note: Price moves provide context; they do not establish what caused a return.

items.label: Jul 13–Aug 6 · APP’s scaling path narrowed
items.text: BofA had cut pixel and advertiser forecasts in July; Q2 showed consumer ad spend, not revenue, up 28% and a shift to partner-led mid-market sales.

items.label: Jul 7–Aug 6 · Unity’s checks were confirmed
items.text: Wells Fargo raised its Vector estimate and a Jefferies survey showed Unity gaining ad-spend share; Q2 showed Strategic Grow up 64%.

sections.heading: The strongest case on each side

items.label: Support
items.text: Unity’s reported Grow and Vector growth matched the checks that preceded it.

items.label: Challenge
items.text: APP’s 28% figure measures ad spend, not revenue, and its self-serve plan gave way to partners; one session cannot separate advertising from other news.

sections.heading: What would have changed the view then

items.label: APP onboarding
items.text: Data showing self-serve advertisers scaling would have eased APP’s execution question; partner-led growth alone would not.

items.label: Unity Grow durability
items.text: A further quarter of Vector gains with a stated revenue contribution would have shown durability; one beat alone could not.

notes.text: Dates show when each source was available; publication times may be unknown.

items.label: The starting view
items.text: Checks pointed to Unity’s Vector gaining advertising business. AppLovin’s outlook depended on adding e-commerce advertisers.

items.label: What was already known
items.text: BofA had cut AppLovin forecasts as advertiser additions slowed. The companies faced different growth tests despite sharing an AI advertising theme.

items.label: What changed
items.text: August 6 results showed AppLovin shifting sales to partners and Unity delivering Grow progress. Their operating results mattered more than the shared label.

items.label: The open question
items.text: Will AppLovin’s partners bring in advertisers, and will Unity sustain Vector’s growth?
